plainEnglish: The Bill of Rights includes the Second Amendment: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” Later cases—not this text alone—define how that applies to federal and state regulation.

links.label: National Archives — Bill of Rights transcript

changed: The Constitution now includes a right of the people to keep and bear arms. It does not yet say how that right limits states, cities, or ordinary gun laws.

plainEnglish: The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees due process and equal protection. It later becomes the vehicle for applying parts of the Bill of Rights—including the Second Amendment—to state and local governments, but that incorporation develops through twentieth-century litigation, not instantly in 1868.
changed: States become bound by the Fourteenth Amendment’s liberty guarantees. That later becomes the path for applying the Second Amendment to state and city gun laws, but not in 1868 itself.

plainEnglish: The Court held the Second Amendment restricts only the federal government, not private actors, and that the federal government could not rely on the Amendment alone to charge individuals for interfering with others’ arms. It did not create a modern individual-rights test for all gun regulation.
changed: The Second Amendment is read as a limit on the federal government, not on private people and not yet on states. Federal prosecutors cannot use it alone to charge private interference with someone else’s arms.

plainEnglish: The Court upheld Illinois’s restriction on private military organizations parading with arms, treating the Second Amendment as tied to militia service and not a license for armed private armies. The decision addressed state police power more than ordinary civilian ownership rules.
changed: A state may ban private military parades. The Court does not treat the Amendment as a license for armed private armies, and it does not yet apply the right against ordinary state gun rules.

plainEnglish: Congress taxes and registers certain firearms and accessories—machine guns, short-barreled rifles and shotguns, silencers, and related items—through the NFA framework enforced with the tax and registration requirements familiar today.
changed: Machine guns, short-barreled rifles and shotguns, and silencers become taxed and registered weapons. Ordinary rifles and handguns stay outside that system.

plainEnglish: Because defendants did not appear, the Court reviewed only the government’s claim that a short-barreled shotgun was not protected without evidence it was ordinary militia equipment. The narrow record limits how far later courts can read Miller as a general rule about all firearms.
changed: A short-barreled shotgun charge can stand when the record never shows the weapon is ordinary militia equipment. The case is narrow: the defendants did not appear, so it is not a full rule for every firearm.

plainEnglish: California bans loaded open carry of firearms in incorporated areas—a state response that tightened public carry rules independently of federal law.
changed: California ends loaded open carry in cities. That is a state rule, not a change in federal law.

plainEnglish: The Gun Control Act creates the federal firearms licensee system, prohibits sales to certain categories of people, sets age floors for dealers, and structures interstate commerce in firearms—establishing the modern federal enforcement baseline.
changed: Dealers must be federally licensed, buyers under set ages are blocked at the counter, and people in prohibited categories cannot legally receive guns through interstate commerce.

plainEnglish: FOPA loosens some federal restrictions—most famously limiting new civilian machine-gun registrations after 1986—while also adding protections for lawful travel and adjusting dealer inspection rules.
changed: Civilian possession of new machine guns is cut off after 1986, while some dealer-inspection and interstate-travel rules are loosened for lawful owners.

plainEnglish: The Brady Act requires federally licensed dealers to run background checks and creates an interim waiting period until the national instant-check system could replace it.
changed: Licensed dealers must run a background check. An interim waiting period fills the gap until a national instant-check system exists.

plainEnglish: Congress bans manufacturing certain semi-automatic rifles with listed features and new magazines over ten rounds, with a ten-year sunset clause. State assault-weapon laws are separate tracks.
changed: For ten years, manufacturers cannot make the listed assault weapons or new magazines over ten rounds. State bans are a separate track and do not depend on this federal sunset.

Congress cannot ban gun possession near a school with no tie to its enumerated powers. The Gun-Free School Zones Act, as then written, falls; Congress later rewrites it to require a commerce connection.
plainEnglish: The Court held the Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeded the Commerce Clause because mere possession of a gun near a school is not economic activity. Federal gun crimes still stand when Congress ties them to interstate commerce.
Federal law expands firearm prohibitions to include misdemeanor crimes of domestic violence and certain protective orders, enforced through the same prohibited-person framework as felonies.
changed: A misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction, and some protective orders, now block firearm possession the way a felony already could.
The Brady Act cannot order local sheriffs to run federal background checks. The check remains a federal duty, which the FBI’s NICS system takes over the next year.
plainEnglish: The Court held the interim Brady provision that required local chief law-enforcement officers to perform background checks violated the Tenth Amendment. Congress may not commandeer state officers to administer a federal gun program.
The FBI’s National Instant Criminal Background Check System starts handling dealer checks nationwide, replacing the Brady interim waiting-period regime for most dealer sales.
changed: The FBI’s instant-check system replaces the Brady waiting period for most dealer sales. A dealer sale now clears or delays through NICS instead of a fixed federal wait.

plainEnglish: The 1994 federal assault-weapons and large-capacity magazine restrictions expire by their own sunset clause when Congress does not renew them, returning federal law to pre-ban baselines while many states keep their own bans.

links.label: Congressional Research Service — AWB sunset context

changed: The federal assault-weapon and magazine limits expire. Those restrictions continue only where a state keeps its own law.

event: Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act
plainEnglish: PLCAA shields firearms manufacturers and dealers from many civil lawsuits arising from criminal misuse of their products, with exceptions for defective products and certain knowing violations of law.
changed: Gun makers and dealers are shielded from many lawsuits that blame them for a third party’s criminal misuse, with exceptions for defects and knowing legal violations.

plainEnglish: The Court held the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess a handgun in the home for self-defense in federal enclaves like D.C., while stressing the right is not unlimited and listing categories of presumptively lawful regulation.
changed: The Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense, at least against the federal government. The right is not unlimited: felon bans, sensitive places, and conditions on commercial sale remain presumptively lawful.

plainEnglish: The Court upheld applying the Lautenberg domestic-violence firearm prohibition to misdemeanor domestic-violence convictions even when the underlying statute was not labeled a “domestic violence” crime, focusing on the conduct proved at trial.
changed: The domestic-violence gun ban reaches a misdemeanor even when the statute is not labeled a domestic-violence law, if the victim was a domestic partner.

plainEnglish: The Court held the Second Amendment applies to state and local governments through the Fourteenth Amendment, incorporating the individual self-defense right recognized in Heller against Chicago’s handgun ban.
changed: States and cities, not just the federal government, must respect the individual right recognized in Heller. Chicago’s handgun ban falls, and state gun laws become subject to the Second Amendment.

plainEnglish: New York expands assault-weapon definitions, magazine limits, and background-check requirements beyond the expired federal ban—a major post-Sandy Hook state tightening.
changed: New York tightens assault-weapon, magazine, and check rules beyond the expired federal ban.
Buying a gun for someone else is still a purchase by the person who fills out the form. A straw purchase stays illegal even when the real recipient could have passed a background check.
plainEnglish: The Court held the federal form’s question about the actual buyer covers someone who buys on behalf of another person. The Gun Control Act’s background-check system looks through the straw purchaser.

In a per curiam decision, the Court reversed a state court that had excluded stun guns from Second Amendment protection merely because they did not exist in 1791, remanding for review under Heller’s framework.
changed: A state cannot exclude a weapon from the Second Amendment merely because it did not exist in 1791. Massachusetts must reconsider its stun-gun ban under Heller.

plainEnglish: The Court held reckless misdemeanor domestic assaults can trigger the Lautenberg firearm prohibition when they meet the statute’s domestic-violence criteria, rejecting a narrow reading limited to intentional crimes only.
changed: A reckless domestic assault, not only an intentional one, can trigger the federal ban on possessing a gun after a misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction.

plainEnglish: ATF amends its regulations to treat bump stocks as machine guns under the National Firearms Act and Gun Control Act, banning new sales and requiring destruction or surrender of existing devices.
changed: ATF classifies bump stocks as machine guns and bans them by rule. That classification lasts until the Supreme Court rejects it in Cargill.

event: N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. City of New York
plainEnglish: The Court dismissed the case as moot after New York City changed its transport rule, issuing no merits ruling on public carry. Later Bruen litigation addressed carry licensing on a fresh record.
changed: The Court decides nothing about the right to carry. New York City changed its transport rule, so the case is dismissed as moot and the later Bruen test is not announced here.

plainEnglish: Texas allows eligible people to carry handguns in public without a license to carry in many places, removing a prior permit requirement for lawful carriers who meet statutory eligibility rules.
changed: Eligible adults in Texas may carry a handgun in many public places without a license. The federal prohibited-person rules still apply.

plainEnglish: ATF updates definitions so certain unfinished frames and receivers and related kits are treated as firearms for marking, licensing, and background-check purposes, targeting ghost-gun assembly without serial numbers.
changed: Many unfinished frames, receivers, and kits are treated as firearms, so they need markings and a background check. Court review of that rule comes later in VanDerStok.

event: N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen
plainEnglish: The Court struck New York’s “proper cause” requirement for public carry licenses and announced a test requiring the government to show a regulation is consistent with the nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.
changed: States cannot demand a special need to carry a handgun in public. A gun law must fit the country’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not a judge’s balancing of safety against the right.

plainEnglish: Congress expands background-check requirements for buyers under 21, clarifies who must register as a federally licensed dealer, and adds state funding for crisis intervention and domestic-violence records in NICS.
changed: Dealer checks expand for buyers under 21, more sellers must get a federal license, and dating-relationship abuse plus mental-health and juvenile records can block a purchase.

plainEnglish: The Court held bump stocks do not qualify as machine guns under the statutory text, invalidating the ATF rule that had banned them and returning the policy question to Congress unless new legislation passes.
changed: Bump stocks are not machine guns under the statute, so the ATF ban falls. Only Congress can put that restriction back.

plainEnglish: The Court upheld a federal prohibition on firearm possession while a domestic-violence restraining order is in force, finding that disarmament fits within the historical tradition test announced in Bruen for this category of orders.
changed: A person subject to a domestic-violence restraining order can still be disarmed while the order is in force. Bruen does not wipe out that traditional limit.
Some weapon-parts kits and unfinished frames count as firearms. Sellers of those ghost-gun kits can be required to serialize them and run a background check.
plainEnglish: The Court held the Gun Control Act can cover weapon parts kits and unfinished frames or receivers that are readily convertible into a working gun. The challenge to ATF’s frames-and-receivers rule fails on that reading of the statute.

changed: A state cannot make licensed public carry a trespass by default on private property open to the public. Hawaii’s rule—no guns in stores, restaurants, and similar places unless the owner expressly allows them—violates the right to carry recognized in Bruen.
plainEnglish: The Court held Hawaii’s affirmative-consent default for carrying on private property open to the public violates the Second and Fourteenth Amendments. Property owners may still ban guns, but the state may not flip the common-law default so that carry is forbidden unless the owner opts in.
